meta.title: AI adoption review checklist for UAE hospitals
meta.description: Questions administrators and nurse leaders can ask when a vendor proposes an AI product: purpose, applicable policy, patient data, security and operations.
meta.lead: Use this when you receive a specific proposal. Tick each item when you have a written answer. The items are the author’s list; the two checklists and the facts page give the sections of the documents behind many of them.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
items: The job the tool will do is described in one sentence and agreed by the department that will use it.
Who will use it, and who will be affected by its output, is listed (including nurses and front-desk staff).
The point where AI enters the process and the role of the physician or practitioner are written down, as the Abu Dhabi AI policy asks.

sections.heading: Regulatory status
items: You have noted which emirate licenses the facility, and therefore whether DoH’s or DHA’s AI policy applies (or both).

The vendor states in writing whether it treats the product as a medical device and which registration it holds; you have asked your regulatory team about the Ministry of Health and Prevention’s requirements.
In Abu Dhabi, the digital product has a named Digital Product Owner and Digital Product Architect, a feasibility study and risk assessment, and a risk tier agreed with the governance group.
A new medical device, or an existing one with cybersecurity considerations, has been or will be evaluated by DoH’s Health Technology Assessment department before implementation.

sections.heading: Patient data
items: The vendor states where data is stored and processed, including logs and backups, and confirms nothing leaves the UAE without DoH authorisation.
The vendor says whether your data is used to train or improve its models, and if so, in what form (anonymised or de-identified) and on what consent basis.
The patient-facing privacy notice, consent wording and withdrawal route are reviewed, including separate consent for sharing data for a specific purpose.
If the tool reads or writes data through the Abu Dhabi health information exchange, the consent clause and the breach clock have been checked against the exchange policy.
The retention period for health data in the tool matches the DoH retention standard, which states a 25-year minimum.

sections.heading: Security and incidents
items: For connected devices and software, you hold the vendor’s MDS2 security disclosure and know how patches and recalls reach you.

The incident card lists the clocks: serious device events within five days, connected-device cyber incidents immediately to the Abu Dhabi Healthcare Cybersecurity Emergency Response Team, and 60 days for patient notice of an exchange breach.
The device is on the connected-device inventory with its software and firmware version.

sections.heading: Performance and fairness
items: The vendor’s validation is described in writing, including data sets used and the limits of the data and algorithm, as Dubai’s policy asks.
Independent third-party validation exists, or the governance group has recorded why it accepts the risk.
You will compare real-world results with the validation results and have agreed what difference triggers a review.
Possible bias is discussed with the vendor, since Dubai’s policy asks for AI that is fair and free of bias.

sections.heading: Operations and people
items: Staff who will use the tool are trained before go-live, including its limits and how to override it.
The tool has a safe fallback, and the vendor explains what happens when its service is down (graceful degradation).
An audit is scheduled, and someone is named to report incidents to DoH or DHA and to the vendor.
